source_text: Ὅταν δὲ ὁ τῶν ἀγώνων παραγένηται καιρὸς, ὅταν ἀνοιγῇ τὸ στάδιον, ὅταν τὸ θέατρον ἄνω καθήμενον ᾖ, ὅταν ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης παρῇ, ἀνάγκη λοιπὸν ἢ ῥᾳθυμήσαντας πεσεῖν καὶ μετὰ αἰσχύνης ἀναχωρῆσαι πολλῆς, ἢ σπουδάσαντας τῶν στεφάνων καὶ τῶν βραβείων ἐπιτυχεῖν. Οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐφ' ὑμῶν, αἱ τριάκοντα ἡμέραι αὗται παλαίστρᾳ τινὶ προσεοίκασι καὶ γυμνασίοις καὶ μελέτῃ. Μάθωμεν ἐντεῦθεν ἤδη περιγενέσθαι τοῦ πονηροῦ δαίμονος ἐκείνου· πρὸς γὰρ ἐκεῖνον ἀποδύεσθαι μέλλομεν μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα, πρὸς ἐκεῖνον πυκτεύειν καὶ μάχεσθαι. Μάθωμεν τοίνυν ἐντεῦθεν ἤδη τὰς λαβὰς ἐκείνου, πόθεν ἐστὶ πονηρὸς, πόθεν ἡμῖν εὐκόλως ἐπηρεάσαι δύναται, ἵνα τῶν ἀγώνων παραγενομένων μὴ ξενοπαθῶμεν μηδὲ θορυβώμεθα, καινὰ τὰ παλαίσματα ὁρῶντες, ἀλλ' ἤδη μεταξὺ ἡμῶν αὐτῶν μελετήσαντες, καὶ τὰς μεθοδείας αὐτοῦ μαθόντες ἁπάσας, μετὰ τοῦ θαῤῥεῖν ἁψώμεθα τῶν παλαισμάτων πρὸς ἐκεῖνον. Πάντοθεν μὲν οὖν ἐπηρεάζειν ἡμῖν εἴωθεν, μάλιστα δὲ διὰ τῆς γλώττης καὶ διὰ τοῦ στόματος. Οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως ἐπιτήδειον ὄργανον ἐκείνῳ πρὸς ἀπάτην καὶ ἀπώλειαν ἡμετέραν, ὡς γλῶττα ἀκόλαστος καὶ στόμα ἀθύρωτον. Ἐντεῦθεν ἡμῖν τὰ πολλὰ πτώματα, ἐντεῦθεν ἡμῖν τὰ χαλεπὰ ἐγκλήματα. Καὶ τὴν μὲν εὐκολίαν τῶν ὀλισθημάτων διὰ τῆς γλώττης τις δηλῶν ἔλεγε· Πολλοὶ ἔπεσον διὰ μαχαίρας, ἀλλ' οὐ τοσοῦτοι ὅσοι διὰ γλώττης. Τὸ δὲ χαλεπὸν τοῦ πτώματος ἐμφαίνων πάλιν ὁ αὐτὸς εἶπεν· Ὀλίσθημα ἀπὸ ἐδάφους μᾶλλον, ἢ ὀλίσθημα ἀπὸ γλώσσης. Ὃ δὲ λέγει τοιοῦτόν ἐστι· Βέλτιόν ἐστι, φησὶ, πεσεῖν καὶ συντριβῆναι τὸ σῶμα, ἢ ῥῆμα προέσθαι τοιοῦτον, ὃ τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν ἀπόλλυσιν. Οὐ λέγει δὲ τὰ πτώματα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ παραινεῖ πολλὴν ποιεῖσθαι πρόνοιαν, ὥστε μὴ ὑποσκελισθῆναι, οὕτως εἰπών· Ποίησον τῷ στόματί σου θύραν καὶ μοχλούς· οὐχ ἵνα θύρας καὶ μοχλοὺς κατασκευάσωμεν, ἀλλ' ἵνα μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς ἀσφαλείας πρὸς τὰ ἄτοπα τῶν ῥημάτων τὴν γλῶτταν ἀποκλείσωμεν. Καὶ πάλιν ἀλλαχοῦ δεικνὺς, ὅτι μετὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας σπουδῆς, καὶ πρὸ τῆς ἡμετέρας τῆς ἄνωθεν δεόμεθα ῥοπῆς, ὥστε τὸ θηρίον τοῦτο κατασχεῖν ἔνδον, πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν τὰς χεῖρας ἀνατείνας ὁ προφήτης ἔλεγεν· Ἔπαρσις τῶν χειρῶν μου θυσία ἑσπερινή. Θοῦ, Κύριε, φυλακὴν τῷ στόματί μου, καὶ θύραν περιοχῆς ἐπὶ τὰ χείλη μου. Ὁ δὲ τὰ πρότερον παραινέσας, πάλιν καὶ αὐτός φησι· Τίς δώσει ἐπὶ τῷ στόματί μου φυλακὴν, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν χειλέων μου σφραγῖδα πανοῦργον; Ὁρᾷς ἕκαστον δεδοικότα τὰ πτώματα ταῦτα, καὶ θρηνοῦντα καὶ συμβουλεύοντα, καὶ εὐχόμενον πολλῆς ἀπολαῦσαι τὴν γλῶτταν φυλακῆς; Καὶ τίνος ἕνεκεν, φησὶν, εἰ τοσοῦτον ἡμῖν φέρει τὸν ὄλεθρον τοῦτο τὸ ὄργανον, ἐνέθηκεν ἡμῖν αὐτὸ παρὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν ὁ Θεός; Ὅτι καὶ πολλὴν ἔχει τὴν ὠφέλειαν· κἂν σπουδάζωμεν, ὠφέλειαν ἔχει μόνον, ὄλεθρον δὲ οὐδένα. Ἄκουσον γοῦν τί φησιν ὁ τὰ πρότερα ἐκεῖνα εἰπών· Ἐν χειρὶ γλώττης ζωὴ καὶ θάνατος. Καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς δὲ τὰ αὐτὰ δηλοῖ λέγων· Ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων σου κατακριθήσῃ, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων σου δικαιωθήσῃ. Μέσῃ γὰρ ἕστηκεν ἡ γλῶσσα τῆς πρὸς ἑκάτερα χρήσεως· σὺ κύριος εἶ. Οὕτω καὶ τὸ ξίφος κεῖται μέσον· κἂν μὲν κατὰ τῶν πολεμίων χρήσῃ σωτήριόν σοι τὸ ὄργανον γέγονεν· ἂν δὲ κατὰ σαυτοῦ τὴν πληγὴν ὠθήσῃς, οὐχ ἡ σιδήρου φύσις, ἀλλ' ἡ σὴ παρανομία γίνεται τῆς σφαγῆς αἰτία.
thought_title: The tongue as the devil's chief weapon
orientation: John Chrysostom is addressing the catechumens about their way of life before baptism, comparing their preparation to athletic training.
pass_a_gloss: But when the time of the contests arrives, when the stadium is opened, when the theater above is seated, when the judge of the contest is present, it is necessary from then on either that those who have been negligent fall and depart with much shame, or that those who have been diligent obtain the crowns and the prizes. So indeed also in your case, these thirty days are like a wrestling school and exercises and practice. Let us learn from now on already to overcome that evil demon; for against him we are about to strip for the contest after baptism, against him to box and to fight. Let us learn therefore from now on already his grips, whence he is evil, whence he is able easily to injure us, so that when the contests arrive we may not be startled nor be troubled, seeing the wrestling moves as new, but having already practiced among ourselves, and having learned all his schemes, with confidence let us engage in the wrestling moves against him. From every side therefore he is accustomed to injure us, but especially through the tongue and through the mouth. For no instrument is so suitable for him for deceit and our destruction as an unbridled tongue and a mouth without doors. From here come to us the many falls, from here come to us the grievous accusations. And someone, showing the ease of the slips through the tongue, said: Many fell by the sword, but not so many as by the tongue. And showing the severity of the fall, the same one said again: A slip from the floor rather than a slip from the tongue. And what he says is of this sort: It is better, he says, to fall and have the body crushed, than to let out such a word which destroys our soul. And he does not speak only of the falls, but also urges that much forethought be made, so as not to be tripped up, having spoken thus: Make for your mouth a door and bars; not so that we may construct doors and bars, but so that with much security we may shut the tongue against the improper words. And again elsewhere showing that with our diligence, and before our diligence, we need the help from above, so as to keep this beast within, the prophet, having lifted up his hands to God, said: The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice. Set, Lord, a guard on my mouth, and a door of enclosure upon my lips. And the one who gave the earlier advice, again he himself says: Who will give a guard upon my mouth, and upon my lips a cunning seal? Do you see each one fearing these falls, and lamenting and advising, and praying that the tongue may enjoy much guarding? And for what reason, he says, if this instrument brings us so much destruction, did God put it in us from the beginning? Because it also has much benefit; and if we are diligent, it has only benefit, and no destruction. Hear then what the one who said those earlier things says: In the hand of the tongue are life and death. And Christ also shows the same things, saying: By your words you will be condemned, and by your words you will be justified. For the tongue stands in the middle of the use toward either side; you are the master. So also the sword lies in the middle; and if you use it against the enemies, the instrument has become your salvation; but if you thrust the blow against yourself, not the nature of the iron, but your own lawlessness becomes the cause of the slaughter.

choices.why: The term refers to the official who presides over athletic contests and awards prizes; rendering it as 'judge of the contest' preserves the athletic imagery Chrysostom is developing.
The verb means to undress, and in athletic contexts refers to the Greek practice of stripping naked for competition; the full phrase preserves the athletic metaphor.
The adjective literally means 'without doors'; keeping the literal sense preserves the image that Chrysostom later develops with the quotation about making a door and bars for the mouth.
The phrase is a literal rendering of the Psalm quotation; 'enclosure' preserves the sense of surrounding and guarding that περιοχή conveys.
The adjective πανοῦργος means crafty or cunning; rendering it literally preserves the paradoxical quality of the request for a seal that is clever enough to keep the lips shut.

choices.term: Ἐν χειρὶ γλώττης ζωὴ καὶ θάνατος
choices.english: In the hand of the tongue are life and death
choices.why: The literal rendering preserves the Hebrew idiom 'in the hand of' meaning 'in the power of', which Chrysostom quotes from Proverbs.

pass_b_english: But when the time of the contests arrives, when the stadium is opened, when the theater above is seated, when the judge of the contest is present, then there is no choice: either you have been careless and you fall and retreat in great shame, or you have trained hard and you win the crowns and the prizes. So it is with you. These thirty days are like a wrestling school, like training grounds, like practice. Let us learn from this moment how to overcome that evil demon. For it is against him that we are going to strip for the contest after baptism; it is against him that we will box and fight. Let us learn from this moment, then, what his grips are, where his evil lies, where he can easily harm us, so that when the contests arrive we are not caught off guard or thrown into confusion at the sight of unfamiliar wrestling moves. Instead, having already practiced among ourselves and learned all his tactics, let us engage him in the wrestling with confidence.

He is accustomed to harm us from every direction, but especially through the tongue and through the mouth. For no instrument is so well suited to him for deceiving us and destroying us as an undisciplined tongue and a mouth without doors. From here come most of our falls; from here come our serious accusations. Someone, showing how easily slips happen through the tongue, said: "Many have fallen by the sword, but not so many as by the tongue" (Sirach 28:18). And the same person, showing how serious the fall is, said: "A slip on the floor is better than a slip of the tongue" (Sirach 20:18). What he means is this: It is better, he says, to fall and break your body than to let out a word that destroys our soul. And he does not only speak of the falls, but he also urges us to take great care so that we are not tripped up, saying: "Make a door and bars for your mouth" (Sirach 28:25)—not so that we build actual doors and bars, but so that with great security we shut the tongue against improper words. And again elsewhere, showing that along with our own effort we need help from above even before our own, the prophet lifted his hands to God and said: "The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice. Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of enclosure over my lips" (Psalm 141:2-3). And the one who gave the earlier advice also says: "Who will set a guard over my mouth, and a cunning seal over my lips?" (Sirach 22:27). Do you see how each one fears these falls, and laments them, and counsels, and prays that the tongue may enjoy great protection?

And why, someone says, if this instrument brings us so much destruction, did God put it in us in the beginning? Because it also has great usefulness. And if we are diligent, it has only usefulness and no destruction at all. Listen, then, to what the one who said those earlier things says: "In the hand of the tongue are life and death" (Proverbs 18:21). And Christ shows the same thing when he says: "By your words you will be condemned, and by your words you will be justified" (Matthew 12:37). For the tongue stands in the middle, able to be used for either purpose. You are its master. So too a sword lies in the middle: if you use it against enemies, the instrument has become your salvation; but if you thrust the blow against yourself, it is not the nature of the iron but your own lawlessness that causes the slaughter.

last_rejected.why: Source asks 'how he is evil' (his nature), not 'where his evil lies' (location).
last_rejected.ruling: πόθεν can mean 'whence/wherefrom' (source/nature), but 'where his evil lies' captures the inquiry into origin/source acceptably.

last_rejected.quote: when the theater above is seated
last_rejected.source_quote: ὅταν τὸ θέατρον ἄνω καθήμενον ᾖ
last_rejected.why: Theater is the spectators, not a building; 'above' means seated aloft/looking down.
last_rejected.fix: when the spectators are seated on high
last_rejected.ruling: ἄνω καθήμενον naturally means seated above; 'theater above is seated' conveys spectators seated aloft adequately.

last_rejected.quote: either you have been careless and you fall
last_rejected.why: Greek is future condition (careless, fall), not past perfect 'have been careless'.
last_rejected.ruling: ῥᾳθυμήσαντας πεσεῖν are aorist participles; 'have been careless and fall' is acceptable English rendering of conditional sequence.

last_rejected.why: ἀθύρωτον means unguarded/unwalled, not 'without doors'; the image is of a city without walls/gates.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀθύρωτον from ἀ- + θύρα (door) means 'without doors'; 'without doors' is literal and intelligible, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the prophet lifted his hands to God and said
last_rejected.why: The source calls David 'the prophet' here, but the English just says 'the prophet' without identifying him as David, though section 5-6 context shows this is David.
last_rejected.fix: the prophet David lifted his hands
last_rejected.ruling: Source says ὁ προφήτης without naming David; English 'the prophet' faithfully reflects source. No identification lost.
